title: The great banking retreat: who will be next to sell up?
full_text:
HSBC’s decision to offload its $36bn Australian home and personal loan portfolio to New York private equity giant Blackstone is less of a tidy corporate exit and more of a signal of something far larger stirring beneath the surface of Australian banking. The tremors are being felt well beyond one foreign lender’s strategic review.
The deal, in which Pepper Money will manage the portfolio and HSBC will wind down its retail business, reflects the brutal reality that competing in Australian mortgages is becoming untenable for anyone without the scale of the big four.
Macquarie has a lot to do with that. The investment bank turned mortgage disrupter has waged an aggressive price war in the home loan market, taking on the majors with rates that have squeezed margins across the board. Macquarie increased its housing market share in the past year from 6.17 per cent to 7.33 per cent and in the year to June it grew its loan book by 27.1 per cent.
It is partly that pressure, sources say, that convinced HSBC it could no longer justify the capital and resources required to stay in the retail fight. Customers with HSBC credit cards or deposit accounts should note they have time on their side, as the bank has stressed no immediate action is required, with the 18-month wind-down designed to give them ample opportunity to find a new home for their money.
But HSBC may not be the last to make such a move. Sources close to the deal say more mid-tier lenders will follow, selling loan portfolios as the competitive environment intensifies.
Bank of Queensland, with its $3.7bn equipment finance sale to Challenger, and Westpac with its $21.7bn RAMS home loan portfolio to KKR, Pimco and Pepper Money have gone down this path. AMP and Bendigo Bank are seen as possible candidates.
For alternative asset managers such as Blackstone, which has more than $1.3 trillion under management globally and appetite for credit, Australian loan portfolios are an attractive proposition and the pipeline could be a long one.
The timing coincides with a softening housing market. New mortgage applications for the National Australia Bank fell 15 per cent in the June quarter, mirroring a slump in auction clearance rates, as reported by The Australian last week. The Reserve Bank’s rate hiking cycle began the downturn, and the Albanese government’s proposed changes to negative gearing and capital gains tax are widely seen as adding further downward pressure.
The outlook for small to medium enterprise banking also is darkening. SME lending, once regarded as an attractive asset class, is facing headwinds as the macro environment bites.
Judo Bank laid bare the challenge when it told the market on June 25 that its cost of risk was expected to come in at $116m to $122m for the 2026 financial year, reflecting an increase in specific provisions. The result was described internally as disappointing and a product of the broader economic environment.
Judo’s cost of risk for the first half of this financial year was $40.1m, compared with $28.8m in the first half of 2025 and $46.7m in the second. The bank is forecasting profit before tax of $163m to $169m for fiscal 2026, rising to $210m to $220m in fiscal 2027.
Judo itself has been floated as a potential acquisition target for Macquarie, which has appointed a new chief executive understood to be focused initially on compliance before some expect him to pivot to mergers and acquisitions for asset management and infrastructure.
But an expansion into banking – potentially through a deal such as Judo – has not been ruled out by close observers of the bank.
What emerges from all of this is a picture of a sector in transition. The big four are consolidating their dominance and Macquarie is sharpening its competitive edge. And those in the middle, such as foreign-owned operations, niche SME lenders and regional banks, have to make choices about where they can compete and where the numbers no longer stack up.
